title: Rejoice always (Philippians 4:4–7)
hookLine: the Lord is near; don't be anxious; the peace that passes understanding

cards: Three in the morning. The ceiling. The list running in your head: the bill, the test result, the thing you said, the thing you didn't say.
Worry is very good at its job. It feels like doing something, and it does nothing. Now consider where these next lines were written.
Not from a beach. Paul is in custody, waiting to learn whether he'll live or die. And the next thing he writes is a command to be glad.

teach.h: IN THE LORD: JOY WITH AN ANCHOR.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice." Note the small words: in the Lord. Paul isn't telling anyone to feel happy about everything that happens.

He's pointing at where the joy is anchored. Then: "Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand." Moderation here is gentleness, a kind of give, the opposite of insisting on your rights.
And the Lord is at hand can be heard two ways, and both may be meant: he is coming soon, and he is close by right now. Then worry.

teach.h: BE CAREFUL FOR NOTHING: DON'T WORRY.
teach.b: The King James says: "Be careful for nothing." In the King James's English, careful meant full of care, anxious. Don't be anxious about anything.
And instead, a practice: "but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." Every thing, small things too.
And notice with thanksgiving tucked in the middle, like a stone in a shoe. You bring the worry, and a thank-you alongside it.

Then the promise: "And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus." The word for keep is a military word. It means to guard, the way soldiers garrison a town.

teach.h: PEACE STANDS GUARD AT THE GATE.
teach.b: Peace stands at the gate of the heart. Not a peace that makes sense of everything.
A peace that goes past understanding, and holds anyway.

how: Philippians 4:4–7 is read in many churches during Advent, and the words about the peace of God are used as a blessing at the end of services in several traditions, including Anglican worship.

o: smile so others never see that you're struggling
feel happy about everything that happens to you
be glad in the Lord, and bring every worry with thanks

games.q: what's inside Philippians 4:4–7 — tap the pairs.
p: guard, like soldiers at a gate

s: be careful for nothing means don't bother being careful
in the old English, careful meant full of care. it means don't be anxious.
Paul wrote these lines while in custody
he was in chains, waiting to learn his fate, as the letter says.
the word for keep is a military word
it means to guard, like a garrison.

games.q: it's three in the morning and a worry won't let go. according to Paul, what do you do?
o: think it through until it's solved.
push it away and think of something else.
bring it to God in prayer, with thanksgiving.
games.why: "in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." then peace stands guard.

practice: Name one worry, the one most likely to wake you tonight, plainly and whole. Then, right beside it, name one thing you're thankful for; it doesn't need to fix the worry, just sit next to it.
If you pray, make both known to God in your own words, as Paul says; if you don't, simply let the two sit together while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Rejoice always. Paul's double command from prison: rejoice in the Lord, again rejoice, and bring every worry with thanksgiving.

orig.note: Greek: peace. the Greek word often carries the fuller sense of the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, all things well.

carryVoice: Your line: the peace that passes understanding. A guard at the gate of the heart. See you tomorrow.
